MSA-01.title: How far ahead of the case count do public data forecast a large dengue season? A retrospective simulation by Brazilian state
MSA-01.abstract: Background: the number of Brazilian states with a high-incidence dengue season (300 or more probable cases per 100,000) ranged from 3 to 19 between 2014/15 and 2024/25. It is not known how far ahead of the simple case count public data allow forecasting this. Methods: retrospective simulation in the 27 states and 11 seasons (297 pairs), each state with its own season, at each of the first 43 weeks, partially rebuilding what was available on each date. Eight predictors (count projection, recent growth, off-season cases, mild winter, thermal suitability, El Niño and, by amendment, cases in the capital and in the interior, each compared with its own history) were tested alone and in pairs, in penalized logistic regressions anchored on the state's history; criterion M chooses, each season, the model with the lowest error in earlier seasons. Lead time is the number of weeks between accuracy stably passing 75% and the count of probable cases making half of the high seasons evident. The main analysis uses the final classification of cases; a sensitivity analysis uses all notifications, as an alternative approximation of what was available. Additional analyses, defined after the first results: a fixed alert rule, a three-state rule with the projection band and a test on held-out seasons. Results: the count projection passed 75% accuracy at week 10, 25 weeks before evidence from the count (95% CI 14 to 30; 11 under the strict rule), and 18 weeks (12 under the strict rule) with the count less dependent on the final classification, in seasons 2016/17 to 2020/21. The interior improved the projection in every version (incremental BSS 0.06 to 0.14), more than off-season cases in most analyses and with a very close value in one of them; the capital added no clear gain to the projection. Criterion M, whose final composition is projection plus interior, had 18 weeks (CI 11 to 29; 10 under the strict rule) in the main analysis and 11 (5 under the strict rule) in the version less dependent on the final classification. The fixed pair projection plus interior had the lowest error and the longest lead time under the strict rule (13 weeks), and was the one chosen when selection used only 2011/12 to 2018/19, but those held-out seasons had already been examined. With a probability alert rule, all models alerted before the count in most high seasons, with false alarms in 37% to 57% of non-high seasons; requiring the whole projection band above the threshold cut false alarms to 0% to 2%, but the median lead time to 0 to 4 weeks, and declared low, in some week, 10% to 25% of the seasons that ended high. Conclusion: in this retrospective simulation, the count projection anticipates evidence from the count; with criterion M, whose final composition is the projection and the cases in the interior (in the retrospective forecasts, M changed models over the seasons), a high season can be forecast 18 weeks ahead of the simple case count in the main analysis, but the lead time falls with the count less dependent on the final classification, and false alarms are frequent. Confirmation depends on the prospective check.
plain: Why did we do this study?

Some years have a lot of dengue and others have little. People who run health services in each state need to know early whether the year will be bad. We wanted to know how much spare time the data the government publishes give before simply adding up the cases makes everything obvious.
What did we do and what did we find?

We went back over eleven past years and pretended to be in each week, using what was already known. We tested eight clues, such as heat, winter, El Niño, cases that show up outside the usual season and cases in the capital and in the rest of the state. The most useful clue was the running total of cases itself, compared with each state's usual pace. It helped even more to check whether the cities outside the capital already had more cases than they usually do. With this, on average, the answer was right in three out of four forecasts some months before the result became obvious. But part of this advantage came from already knowing which cases would later be ruled out. A simple alert would also raise many alarms for nothing, and a more cautious alert almost never raises alarms for nothing, but comes late and sometimes says the year will be calm when it will not.
Public data already give an early warning, but the test looked back in time. It still has to be seen whether it works in the coming years. This note says nothing about the health of any person.

Steps with AI: literature search, protocol design, all code (collection, database, signals, models, evaluation, figures), running the analyses, writing and translation into English and Spanish. Checking: automatic only: the code runs end to end from raw files with SHA-256 hashes; the numbers in the text were checked by script against the result files; DOIs and links were verified. There was no independent human validation of the AI steps, and the results may contain errors or gaps because of this; the author reviewed the final text. Tool limitations: it can make mistakes in code and in reading the literature that automatic checks do not catch. Record: protocol, code and results versioned in the program's public repository (github.com/willianwistuba/mais-saude-ai), with the protocol in commit a9c960e, the 2026/27 forecast in commit dba78f5, amendment 6 in commit 3149434, its results in commit 252e1a5 and amendment 7, with its results, in commit c054974. Conflicts and funding: none.

MSA-02.title: Pooled testing for HIV viral load: simulation of reaction use and time to confirmation of failure, with parameters from the Brazilian public network
MSA-02.short: Pooled testing for HIV viral load
MSA-02.abstract: Background: in HIV treatment programs with high viral suppression, most routine viral load tests fall below the failure cutoff. In Brazil, about 89% of results from people on treatment for six months or more are below 50 copies/mL, and the public network contracts around 1.1 million tests per year. Testing samples in pools saves reactions, but dilution, low-level viremia and residual RNA below 50 copies/mL may delay the detection of failure at the 200 cutoff or consume the savings. This note records the technique and estimates its potential, using Brazilian parameters as a reference case. Methods: simulation with the national viral load distribution (2022), detectable residual RNA in 25% of collections below 50 copies/mL in the main scenario, drawn between 1 and 49 copies/mL (in the sensitivity analysis, shares from 0% to 40% and ranges from 20 to 49 and from 40 to 49) and the detection, quantification and reproducibility described in the instructions for use of the network kits (cobas HIV-1 on the 5800 and 4800 systems). Retest rules were restricted to those the kit allows to be executed: retest only pools quantified at 20 cp/mL or more (rule Q20, main) or any detected pool (rule D). In the cross-sectional stage (400,000 collections), strategies were compared by subrange, with discordances in both directions. In the longitudinal stage, a cohort of 200,000 suppressed adults was followed for 24 months, with collections every six months, confirmation in a new collection 28 days after the report and the same 17,301 episodes in both arms. Variation comes from 40 replicates. Results: pools of 4 with rule Q20 used 39.7% fewer reactions per collection (empirical interval across replicates 39.5% to 40.0%) and 50.4% fewer during follow-up (50.3% to 50.5%), with a simulated difference close to zero in confirmation within 60 days (0.0 point; −0.3 to 0.2) and a median of 47 days until confirmation, against 42 for individual testing. In the residual RNA scenarios tested, rule Q20 saved 26% to 42% of reactions per collection and 35% to 53% during follow-up; rule D, from 38% to nothing. Just above the cutoff, confirmation within 60 days had wide intervals (rebounds of 200 to 249: −1.0 point; −6.7 to 4.2) and fell by about 3 points between 200 and 299 with greater imprecision. Quantitative deconvolution saved 56% of reactions, but detected only 35.0% of loads between 200 and 249, against 65.5% for individual testing. Pre-concentration of plasma showed no advantage: with rule D, it saved 6% to 7%; with a trigger equivalent to that of Q20, it tied with the ordinary pool. Conclusion: in this simulation, retesting only quantified pools kept savings in all the scenarios tested, from 26% to 53% of reactions, with a magnitude sensitive to the distribution of loads below 50, and confirmation of failure close to that of individual testing overall, with more uncertainty just above the cutoff. The cost reduction compared with current practice would be a fraction of these percentages, proportional to the eligible fraction and to the weight of the reaction in the price, and would depend on laboratory validation, on admission of the procedure and on payment linked to the number of reactions.
plain: Why did we do this study?

People who live with HIV and take treatment repeat a blood test a few times a year to see if the virus is under control. Almost always the result says there is no virus. We wanted to know if it is possible to use fewer tests without taking longer to find out when the treatment stops working.
What did we do and what did we find?

We used a computer to try out an old idea: mix a little of the blood of four people and test the mix only once. If the mix shows little or no virus, no one in the group needs a new test. If it shows real virus, each person is tested alone. We used the numbers of the test used in Brazil. Many people on treatment still have a tiny bit of virus left in the blood. So the rule that worked only repeats the test when the mix has enough virus to be counted. This way, the idea would use between a quarter and a half fewer tests. Almost all the problem cases would be confirmed in the same time, with about five more days of waiting. When the virus came back only a little, the group may let a few more cases slip through.

The idea works well on the computer, but it still needs to be tried in a lab. To turn into money saved, rules and the way the tests are paid for would also need to change, and only part of the tests could use the idea. The note keeps the numbers on record for when this is possible. It says nothing about the health of any person.
MSA-02.ai_card: Tools: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), in sessions on Nov 8 and 9, 2026 (versions 1, 1.1 and 1.2). Steps with AI: formulation of the hypotheses, literature search, queries to the National Public Procurement Portal, reading of the public documents and of the kits' instructions for use, writing of all the code, running of the simulations, writing and translation into English and Spanish. Checking: automatic only: the numbers in the text were copied from the scripts' outputs, and the published scripts were run again to check that they reproduce those outputs; the detection model was compared with the tables in the instructions for use; excerpts from documents were checked by reading the PDFs. Reviews by another AI tool pointed out problems that were corrected before version 1 and, after it, the premise of zero load below 50 cp/mL, corrected in version 1.1; a second review pointed out the dependence on the range of residual RNA, the loss just above the cutoff and pre-concentration tested only with rule D, addressed in version 1.2; the calculations of both reviews were reproduced with the code published before the corrections. There was no independent human validation of the steps carried out by AI, and the results may contain errors or gaps because of this; the author reviews the final text. Tool limitations: it may make mistakes in code, in reading figures and in reading literature without the error showing up in the automatic checks. Record: code and outputs versioned in the program's public repository (github.com/willianwistuba/mais-saude-ai), in codigo_src/msa02_*.py and dados/msa02/; there was no protocol registered before the analyses. Conflicts and funding: none.

items.short: Why does dengue come in waves?
items.title: Why does dengue come in waves instead of the same every year?
items.text: Brazil alternates years of very large epidemics with calmer years, and climate alone does not explain this rhythm. There are four types of the virus, and infection by one protects against the others only for a while. Three explanations compete: this temporary protection, the higher severity and transmission of the second infection, and climate. The plan is to make them compete using more than two decades of Brazilian public data and to estimate how long cross-protection between the virus types lasts here.

method_page.h1: How does Mais Saúde AI work?
method_page.lead: A health informatics program: using public data, open code and artificial intelligence with automated checks to organize health information and test hypotheses about populations, with enough rigor for any specialist to check every number.
method_page.body:
Who writes?

{byline}

The author is an independent researcher and not a health professional. The project is individual, with no co-author or health reviewer. Research and construction are carried out with AI, and the author reviews the final text before publication. There is no independent human validation of the research steps carried out with AI: they are checked automatically (tests, public benchmarks, verification of links and DOIs against the sources), and results may contain errors or gaps as a consequence. Only what passes these checks is published.

What does the project do?

  • Collects, cleans, versions and documents public health data.
  • Organizes and synthesizes published scientific literature.
  • Builds population-level mathematical and statistical models, such as epidemics, queues and costs.
  • Publishes hypotheses as hypotheses, together with the test that would confirm or refute them.
  • Rewrites official documents in plain language, always next to the original text.

What does the project never do?

  • Advise, diagnose, give a prognosis or recommend treatment to anyone.
  • Offer a tool that takes a patient's data and returns a diagnosis, risk with a course of action, a dose or triage.
  • Calculate drug doses or interpret anyone's test results.
  • Receive or store data that identify people.
  • Accept resources from manufacturers of technologies it assesses or comments on.

There is no consultation service. Messages asking for advice on a personal case receive a standard reply referring the person to a health professional.

The role of artificial intelligence

Language models take part in literature search, programming, information extraction and classification, writing and translation. AI is not an author, and the author is responsible for everything published. Each note includes an AI use statement with the tools and versions used, the steps in which they acted, how outputs were checked and with what error rate, known limitations, and an archive of the raw prompts and outputs. In literature syntheses, the deviation from the two-human-reviewer standard is declared: the work is called an AI-assisted synthesis with a single human reviewer, and the agreement between AI and author is published.

Rigor

  • Question, sources, method and success criterion are registered with a date before looking at the results.
  • Every published finding carries a 95% confidence interval, and multiple comparisons in the same study are corrected.
  • Models are evaluated outside the data used to fit them.
  • What matches the literature is credited; reproducing a known result validates the method and is not a novelty.
  • Negative results and rejected hypotheses are published with the same care as positive ones.
  • Each note follows the applicable reporting guideline, such as STROBE, RECORD, PRISMA or EPIFORGE, and attaches its checklist.

Data and privacy

Only public, aggregated data that do not identify individuals are used, such as those from DATASUS. Counts below five are suppressed at municipal level, and no re-identification is attempted. For this reason the notes are exempt from ethics committee review under Brazilian National Health Council Resolution 510/2016 and CONEP Circular Letter 17/2022. Before each automated download, the source's terms of use are read and respected, preferring official APIs and open data portals.

Format and publication

Notes follow the conventions of scientific articles: title, authorship, date and version, plain-language summary, technical abstract, keywords, numbered sections, figures and tables, numbered citations, references and closing statements on AI use, data, ethics and competing interests. The PDF is typeset in two columns with REVTeX. The original is written in Portuguese; the English and Spanish versions are translations reviewed by the author. Each note receives a DOI on Zenodo, under CC BY 4.0 for text and data and the MIT license for code.

Corrections

An error found becomes a new version, with a revision note at the top explaining what changed and what did not. The previous version remains accessible. Nothing is deleted silently.

Standard note disclaimer

Every published text displays the disclaimer below.
